paper_title: Skip the Compressor: Coding Agents Fix More Issues When They Pick Whole Files

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A coding agent works on repositories that can be far larger than its context window can hold. Prompt compressors and retrievers offer solutions to this problem, but patching an issue needs two things at once: the files that must change, and their code exactly as written, since the model must reproduce the lines it edits. Retrievers rank code by its similarity to the issue rather than by whether it must change, and compressors delete text to fit the budget. We show that at an equal token budget, an agent resolves more issues when the budget goes to choosing which files to show verbatim, as our simple selector CQ2-CARE does, than when it goes to pruning tokens or retrieving chunks. We fit every context to the same per-issue budget on 300 recent SWE-rebench issues and grade each patch with the benchmark's tests. With GPT-5.6 and Claude Opus 5, CQ2-CARE resolves 43.7% and 46.7% of the issues, 6.3 points more than the best of three compressors with either model, and 9.3 and 12.7 points more than the best of three retrievers. CQ2-CARE even resolves more issues than two methods trained for issue resolution, SweRank (by 0.7 and 1.7 points) and SWE-Pruner (by 2.0 and 7.3). Our analysis shows the defects of the baseline methods: retrievers often miss the files to edit, and compressors keep them but alter their text, so fewer patches apply. Exact-file selection needs no compression model and shows every line as the repository has it, so the model can quote the code it edits.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs) now resolve real software issues end to end: they read an issue, explore repository and write patch that the projects tests accept (Jimenez et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2025). Managing what enters their context already *Equal contribution. 1 makes them cheaper: it can halve an agents cost (Lindenbauer et al., 2025) or cut it by fifth to third (Xiao et al., 2026). Every prompt token is paid for on every call, and models use information in the middle of long input less reliably than at its ends (Liu et al., 2024). Yet every step still needs code in the prompt, and coding agents context window is small next to the repositories it works on: SWE-bench codebases average 3,010 non-test files and 438K lines (Jimenez et al., 2024). We therefore treat the repository as the agents memory and the prompt as compressed view of it, one that leaves most of the code out. To resolve an issue, the view still has to keep two things: the files the fix must edit, and their text exactly as it is. For anyone building coding agent, this raises practical question: at fixed token budget, which compression of the repository lets the model resolve the most issues? Three lines of work each study part of this question: prompt compression for long naturallanguage prompts (Jiang et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2024), retrieval of repository code for code completion and issue resolution (Zhang et al., 2023; Jimenez et al., 2024), and issue-resolution systems that prune what an agent reads (Wang et al., 2026) or compress the context around known fault locations (Jia et al., 2026). Figure 1 shows how the first two can fail on one issue from our study, report that some error messages lack the of an f-string. chunk retriever fills the budget with the repositorys issue templates, which share the reports wording, and never shows the file to edit. token pruner keeps that file but deletes prefixes and quotation marks, so the models patch rewrites line that does not exist and fails to apply. Shown the file whole and verbatim, the same model writes the fix. None of these lines of work compares retrieval, token pruning and file selection at matched budget per issue, with each method free to decide which files enter the context. Figure 1: An issue sample under different compression methods. The issue (pypa__twine-1225) reports error messages that lack the of an f-string; the gold patch edits twine/sdist.py. ρ: gold-file recall, the share of the gold-patch files in the context m; ε: the share of ms lines that are verbatim. BM25 fills Bi with issue templates (two of three spans shown), so its patch guesses lines it never saw; LLMLingua-2 deletes tokens (struck out), among them the of line 23, so its patch rewrites line that does not exist; ours shows the file verbatim. Indentation is trimmed; an ellipsis marks an elided prefix. Chosen for illustration as the smallest of the 4 such issues out of 300 (a random one is in Appendix A). Right: resolution with GPT-5.6 (solid) and Claude Opus 5 (light), every context fitted to Bi. SWE-Pruner, line pruner trained for coding agents, is the last bar of the pruning group, and SweRank, trained retriever of whole functions, the last bar of the retrieval group. Both failures follow from how these tools work. Retrievers rank chunks or files by their similarity to the issue (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009; Jimenez et al., 2024; Suresh et al., 2025), so text that echoes the report can outrank the file to edit. Prompt compressors delete the tokens or code blocks that small model scores as least useful (Jiang et al., 2023, 2024; Pan et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025); this costs little when the output is an answer or summary, but an edit must quote the code it changes exactly (Xia et al., 2025; Anthropic, 2024; Gauthier, 2026). The remedy follows: spend the budget on choosing which files to show, and show them whole and verbatim, so that edits quote text that exists and no compression model runs in the loop. Since each chosen file is shown whole, the selector must name few files, and the right ones. We therefore build simple selector, CQ2-CARE, that asks the model under test twice, independently, which files must change and keeps the files both answers name, taking agreement between samples as sign of reliability (Wang et al., 2023); it then adds the short spans that grep finds for definitions, callers or strings the model requests, so code the fix depends on is shown verbatim even outside the chosen files. Its strength is its choice of unit, not its sampling scheme: single answer cut to the same number of files does about as well, so what matters is choosing few files well (4.4). We test this remedy in controlled comparison on 300 issues from the SWE-rebench leaderboard (Badertdinov et al., 2025), one per repository: fixed model receives the issue and one context fitted to the size of the CQ2-CARE context for that issue, writes one patch, and the benchmarks harness grades it with the issues tests. We describe each context by its gold-file recall, the share of the files to edit that it contains, and by the share of its lines that are verbatim, and we run controlled tests that change one of the two at time. With each of two model families, the selector resolves more issues than each of three compressors and three retrievers, among them SWE-benchs file-level BM25; with Claude, its lead over one compressor, LLMLingua-2, is narrow. The losses separate cleanly: retrievers keep the text verbatim but often miss the files to edit, and token pruners keep those files but alter their text, so fewer patches apply. Controlled tests show that each loss costs on its own: deleting tokens from the selectors own contexts, with the files unchanged, costs about as much as the compressors lose in the main comparison, while compressor that keeps whole lines matches the selector when it starts from the same files. The selector even resolves more issues than two methods trained for issue resolution: SWE-Pruner, 2 line pruner, and SweRank, retriever that shows whole functions verbatim and comes within two points. Our contributions are as follows: CQ2-CARE, simple selector that spends the context budget on the files the model names and shows them verbatim, with no compression model (2). budget-matched, test-graded comparison of CQ2-CARE with three prompt compressors, three retrievers, among them SWE-benchs filelevel BM25, and two methods trained for issue resolution, on 300 issues and two model families (3.3). decomposition of the losses into gold-file recall and verbatim lines, with controlled tests that change one at time (4.14.2).

sections.title: 3.1 Data
sections.content: We use the SWE-rebench leaderboard (Badertdinov et al., 2025), which collects recent issues automatically, at pinned revision with 860 Python tasks from 413 repositories; on the older SWE-bench Verified, models can often name the files to edit from the issue text alone, which its authors attribute in part to possible memorization (Liang et al., 2026). salted hash drew 340 candidate issues, one per repository, before any model call. Each candidate passed an eligibility check in our harness: the gold patch resolves it and an empty patch does not (328 of 340 passed). The first 300 eligible issues form the population, created between January 2025 and May 2026; hash-chosen subset of 100 is used for the rate sweep and the edit-format control.

sections.title: 3.2 Setup and Baselines
sections.content: All methods share one pipeline and differ only in the context step (Appendix B). CQ2-CARE (2) draws five ranked answers per issue, of which salted hash picks L1, L2 and L0; with GPT-5.6, its context holds 1.7 selected files on average (median 1) and spans from 6.0 more files (variants in 4.4). The baselines are context steps an agent builder can drop in without training. Each compressor cuts m, the uncompressed context that the same pipeline builds from L0 alone, to Bi and keeps span headers verbatim ( already fits in 52 issues and is used as is). We run the official implementations with their documented settings: LLMLingua-2 (Pan et al., 2024), LongLLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2024) with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen Team et al., 2025) as the scorer, and LongCodeZip (Shi et al., 2025) with Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (Hui et al., 2024). Chunk BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009) and dense retrieval with CodeRankEmbed (Suresh et al., 2025) rank top-level Python definitions or 60-line windows against the issue and pack them in rank order up to Bi. File-level BM25, SWEbenchs own retrieval baseline (Jimenez et al., 2024), adds whole non-test Python files in rank order while they fit, so it lands under Bi. Two methods trained for issue resolution were added after the main results, with the same prompt and grader and without tests, gold patches or fault locations (Algorithms 6 and 9): SWE-Pruner (Wang et al., 2026) deletes lines from the single-draw context that the compressors cut at threshold that fits Bi, and SweRank (Reddy et al., 2026) ranks every non-test Python function against the issue; we show whole functions in that order up to Bi. For scale, the gold-file oracle (upper bound) shows the source files the gold patch modifies, and the no-source context shows the issue alone. The main table reports one model per family, each used for every call: gpt-5.6-sol (medium reasoning effort) and Claude Opus 5, both on all 300 issues. The model returns unified diff from prompt that differs across contexts only in the localized paths and the context, and we grade it with the SWE-rebench fork of the official harness (Jimenez et al., 2024; Badertdinov et al., 2025); patches that fail to parse or apply count as unresolved (exit codes alone are not enough; Appendix C). sections.title: 3.3 Main Results
sections.content: Exact files beat every drop-in baseline with both models  (Table 1)  . CQ2-CARE resolves 43.7% of the issues with GPT-5.6 and 46.7% with Claude Opus 5, 6.3 points more than the best compressor with either model and 9.3 and 12.7 points more than the best retriever. All these leads are significant, the narrowest (LLMLingua-2 with Claude, = 0.027) only weakly. Whole files alone are not enough: SWE-benchs file-level BM25 shows whole files chosen by similarity to the issue and trails by 9.3 and 12.7 points. CQ2-CARE even resolves more issues than the two trained methods: SWE-Pruner trails with both models, significantly only with Claude, and SweRank is within two points (4.1). Exact files chosen by the model come close to the true ones: the gold files resolve 5.7 points more than CQ2-CARE with GPT-5.6 and no more with Claude. At the budget compressor would use, an agent that chooses few whole files recovers most of what knowing the files to edit would give it.

sections.title: 4.4 Ablations of CQ2-CARE
sections.content: What makes exact-file selection work is predicting few files, not agreement between samples (Appendix Table 6). Agreement raises localization F1 well above single draw (0.613 vs. 0.430), but only because it names half as many files: single draw cut to the same number of files reaches 0.600 and resolves about as many issues with both models (Claude: Appendix Table 17). More exact files help when the budget allows: the files that either draw names resolve 4.0 points more than CQ2-CARE at 2.3K more tokens, and the agreement thresholds tof-5 trade files for tokens smoothly (Figure 3). The evidence step adds 3.0 points, short of significance (p = 0.068). Exact-file selection is also the cheaper way to fill the budget. Against the uncompressed single draw, CQ2-CARE uses 0.68 the tokens with GPT-5.6 and passes the planned non-inferiority test; with Claude, it uses 0.73 the tokens and resolves more, but the token ratios upper bound narrowly misses its margin (Appendix D). Its whole pipeline costs $0.151 per issue with GPT-5.6, against $0.199 for the single draw and $0.1680.177 for the compressor contexts in API calls alone, because those first build the uncompressed context.

sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: Choose files or compress tokens? An agent builder who must cut context can retrieve chunks, prune larger context, or choose files and show them whole. Retrieval keeps the text but often loses the files to edit, and token pruning keeps the files but alters the text that an edit must quote; each costs on its own (4.2). Edits stay locatable only when the text is verbatim (4.3), and editing tools that replace quoted span (Anthropic, 2024; Gauthier, 2026) or numbered line range (Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025) need exactly this. Choosing files also needs no compression model: LongLLMLingua and LongCodeZip spent median 3437 of GPU time per issue (8497 on Claudes larger contexts, where LongCodeZip ran out of memory on 4 issues at 48 GB), and CQ2-CARE adds one localization call. What the results do not show is that selector beats code-aware compressor that starts from the same files: given our candidates, LongCodeZip matched CQ2-CARE, although it still spent 6.8 GPU-hours on 300 issues. We read this as rule rather than ranking: choose the candidate files well, then cut whole lines if anything must be cut. Re-read on demand or compress once? Agents that can re-open files may recover some of the losses we measure, because compressed view tells them which file to read in full. Each re-read, however, costs turn and the tokens that compression was meant to save, and model may not notice that the text it sees is altered: in Figure 1, it rewrote line that does not exist in the file. Measuring this trade-off needs full agent loop, which we leave to future work. Localization scores or end-to-end tests? Intermediate metrics can mislead. Agreement between two localization samples raises file-level F1 far above single sample, yet single sample cut to the same number of files resolves about as many issues (4.4). Exit-code grading, which we used before this study, credited an empty patch on 4 of 6 issues (Appendix C). Context methods for coding agents should therefore be compared end to end, at equal budgets, with the benchmarks tests.

sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: Prompt compression. Hard prompt compression removes tokens or sentences that smaller model judges uninformative (Li et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023, 2024; Pan et al., 2024); RECOMP compresses retrieved documents extractively or abstractively (Xu et al., 2024), and Li et al. (2025) survey the area. On long-context question answering and summarization, Jha et al. (2024) find that extractive, reranker-based selection of chunks often outperforms token pruning and abstractive summarization. We find the same ordering for issue resolution and identify the cost specific to it: edits must quote the text that pruning alters. Agent memory. Language-agent frameworks separate working memory, from which each prompt is built, from long-term memories retrieved into it (Sumers et al., 2024), and MemGPT manages what moves between limited context and external storage (Packer et al., 2024); for coding agent, the repository is the long-term memory, and the question is which part of it enters the prompt. For code, LongCodeZip keeps whole functions and blocks chosen by perplexity, since its authors note that token-level compression corrupts code syntax and structure (Shi et al., 2025), and perplexity-based pruning removes Python indentation in repository-level completion (Feng et al., 2026). SWEzze trains compressor on executionderived minimal contexts, but compares methods only around fault locations already found by Agentless (Jia et al., 2026); SWE-Pruner prunes the lines an agent reads and attributes, as hypothesis, the losses of LLMLingua-2 and embedding retrieval in 50-issue comparison to disrupted syntax and missed details (Wang et al., 2026). SweRank learns to retrieve and rerank whole functions from issue patch pairs (Reddy et al., 2026). We instead fix the budget per issue, let each method decide which files enter the context, and measure both failure modes with controlled tests.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We compared ways to fill coding agents context budget at equal per-issue budgets on 300 testgraded issues with two model families. Showing few whole files verbatim resolved more issues than pruning tokens or retrieving chunks, and about as many as trained retriever of whole functions, because retrieval often misses the files to edit and to8 ken pruning alters the text that patches must quote, and controlled tests showed that each loss costs on its own. For coding agents, the context budget is best spent choosing which code to show, kept verbatim and in whole lines.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Setting. We study one patch call per context on Python issues from one benchmark, not multiturn agent that could read more files or run tests. Comparisons. Bi is our contexts realized size, so we compare at our methods operating point (the 100-issue rate sweep covers others). Filelevel BM25, the controlled tests, SWE-Pruner (in its single-turn mode) and SweRank were added after the main results; SweRank may have trained on other pull requests from our repositories, and its small gap to CQ2-CARE does not show equal performance. Estimator. It uses the gold patch and serves only as diagnostic; its coverage counted inside functions was chosen after seeing SweRanks result and needs test on an unseen method. Precision and contamination. Most cells have one patch sample, and second one flips 8.7 18.9% of outcomes, so small gaps such as Claudes to LLMLingua-2 (p = 0.027) are fragile. The issues may overlap the models training data, but the gaps do not shrink detectably on newer issues (Appendix Table 18a); some may come from repositories seen while developing CQ2-CARE.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: This work evaluates context-compression methods on public open-source repositories and issues. It involves no human subjects or personal data. Generated patches were executed only inside isolated sandboxes. We will release code, prompts and perissue outcomes.

sections.title: Learned
sections.content: Grading with exit codes is not grading resolution. Before this study, our resolution numbers came from an executor that marked an issue resolved when the repositorys test command exited with code 0, without applying the issues test patch or checking the FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS lists. On 6 issues we checked, an empty patch counted as resolved on 4 under that rule and on 0 under official grading. That rule largely measures whether the existing test suite passes. All results in this paper use official grading, and every issue was checked in advance to be resolved by its gold patch and not by an empty patch. Budget matching is fiddly. Rate knobs are coarse (LLMLingua-2 quantizes its threshold to 1%; LongCodeZips rate cannot be set to 1.0 because of an upstream bug), so we search fixed grid with interpolation and record misses rather than rerunning with other settings. Span headers count toward the budget and are kept verbatim for every method, so compressors never lose file identity. Infrastructure. Model-based compressors ran out of memory on the largest contexts; we released GPU memory between issues and retried those issues in fresh process with expandable memory segments, and LongCodeZip still failed on 4 of Claudes 300 contexts, even on 48 GB A6000 (counted as unresolved; in the worst case Algorithm 5 LongCodeZip (Shi et al., 2025): function-level then block-level pruning for code with Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, budget-matched with Algorithm 2 on its rate. With Claude, one issues tests hung in two separate grading runs for every context, although they had passed in the eligibility check; it is counted as unresolved for all contexts, which leaves every paired contrast unchanged. Parallel container builds into cold shared cache corrupted it, so builds are serialized. H1 (CQ2-CARE vs. the three compressors) and H2 (vs. the other budget-matched exact-text contexts: the size-matched single draw, chunk BM25 and dense retrieval) use one-sided exact McNemar tests with Holm correction within each family; H3 tests the evidence step; H4 tests non-inferiority to the uncompressed single-draw context (lower 95% bound of the resolution ratio above 0.85 and upper bound of the token ratio below 0.75).
